idiom_name: Twirl compiled templates + Play content negotiation (Html/Json/XML writeables)
implementation_notes: Twirl compiles every template into a Scala function returning a typed content value - Html, Xml, Txt, Csv - so stage one is a view-model case class and stage two is that function plus Play's Writeable instance that serialises the content type into the response. Play's documentation notes templates can generate any text-based format, and the same case class feeds an HTML template or a Json.toJson writes instance, with the channel chosen by content negotiation or an explicit route. Escaping is per content type (HTML/XML escaped by default, Html(...) marks trusted fragments), so keep channel-specific markup inside the template and the case class free of both template and serialiser concerns. Template parameters are the page contract; with templateImports and injected components, a template can also depend on shared renderers without touching the model.
code_sketch:
case class InvoiceVm(customer: String, total: String)   // stage 1: logical page

// app/views/invoice.scala.html:  @(vm: InvoiceVm) ...   // compiled to a function
val html: Html = views.html.invoice(vm)                 // stage 2: HTML channel
val json = Json.toJson(vm)                              // JSON channel, same page
Ok(html).as(HTML)      // or Ok(json).as(JSON): the writeable is the renderer
pitfalls: Compiled templates turn template errors into build errors, but a template change forces a rebuild - per tenant HTML belongs in data, not in templates.
Html(...)/@Html(...) marks content as trusted; injecting user data there is the standard XSS route, and a fragment escaped for HTML is wrong in a text or XML template.
Passing a domain entity instead of a view model drags business types and lazy state into the renderer, so the template ends up calling the database.
